# Two front doors, one backend

<sub>Self-contained edition — the four animated diagrams are embedded in this file, so it can be moved, emailed or opened on its own with nothing else alongside it. <b>GitHub strips <code>data:</code> image sources</b>, so for a repository README use <a href="ARCHITECTURE.md">ARCHITECTURE.md</a>, which points at the same diagrams as separate files.</sub>

A booking form and an AI receptionist both create appointments. They share a
single service layer, a single availability engine, and a single database
constraint — so the two can never disagree about what is free.

These four plates trace that path from the browser down to the row that makes
double booking impossible. **The diagrams are animated:** moving dashes show the
direction data actually flows.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Browser** | Next.js 15 · React 19 · Tailwind · Socket.IO client |
| **API** | Express · TypeScript · Socket.IO · JWT |
| **Data** | PostgreSQL 17 |
| **Model** | Mistral, via tool calling |

---

## Plate 01 — The whole system

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,">
  <img alt="Browser clients reach an Express API over REST and WebSocket. Controllers call services, services call repositories, and repositories are the only code that talks to PostgreSQL. The AI service calls Mistral for tool decisions but never the database." src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," width="100%">
</picture>

Three clients, one entry point. Controllers stay thin — they validate,
authenticate and hand off. **Every business rule lives in the service layer**,
which never touches `req` or `res`, so the same function serves an HTTP request,
a websocket event, or an AI tool call unchanged. Repositories are the only code
that writes SQL.

Reading the wires: teal is a request path, dashed teal is persistent or
bidirectional, amber reaches the database.

---

## Plate 02 — Why the chatbot cannot drift from the booking form

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,">
  <img alt="The booking form calls POST /api/appointments and the chatbot's create_appointment tool calls the same appointmentService.create function, so both paths share one set of rules and one database constraint." src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," width="100%">
</picture>

The assistant has no booking logic of its own. Its `create_appointment` tool
calls the very function the REST endpoint calls — same validation, same
availability check, same transaction, same constraint.

**Verified end to end:** the test suite books through the chat socket, then
fetches that appointment over REST and confirms the slot has disappeared from
public availability. There is no second booking path to keep in sync.

---

## Plate 03 — Where the double-booking guarantee actually lives

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,">
  <img alt="Two concurrent requests both pass the application availability check because neither has committed yet. PostgreSQL's exclusion constraint accepts the first insert and rejects the second with SQLSTATE 23P01, which the service turns into a 409 offering alternative times." src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," width="100%">
</picture>

Checking availability before inserting is **not** sufficient — two transactions
can both read the same free slot before either writes. The rule is therefore
enforced by the storage engine:

```sql
ALTER TABLE appointments
    ADD CONSTRAINT appointments_no_overlap
    EXCLUDE USING gist (
        appointment_date WITH =,
        timerange(start_time, end_time, '[)') WITH &&
    )
    WHERE (status <> 'CANCELLED');
```

PostgreSQL takes the predicate locks itself, so the second concurrent insert
fails with `SQLSTATE 23P01` no matter how the race is timed. The service catches
that code and returns a `409` carrying the nearest free times.

The same predicate — `status <> 'CANCELLED'` — appears in the constraint *and*
in the availability query, so the two cannot drift apart. A completed
appointment keeps its slot; only a cancellation releases it.

> **Verified:** 8 simultaneous requests for one slot → exactly 1 succeeds,
> 7 rejected with `409`.

## Plate 04 — What the model is allowed to touch

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,">
  <img alt="The language model only chooses tool names and arguments. Tools validate arguments and delegate to services, which own the rules and reach the database. The model itself never crosses into the data layer." src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," width="100%">
</picture>

The model decides *which* tool to call. It never decides whether a slot is free,
whose appointment it may read, or what the clinic charges — those answers come
from services and from retrieval.

| Tool | Delegates to |
| --- | --- |
| `check_available_slots` | `availabilityService.getDayAvailability` |
| `get_clinic_information` | `knowledgeService.retrieve` (RAG) |
| `create_appointment` | `appointmentService.create` |
| `get_my_appointments` | `appointmentService.listForUser` |
| `cancel_appointment` | `appointmentService.cancel` |
| `reschedule_appointment` | `appointmentService.reschedule` |
| `find_next_available` | `availabilityService.findNextAvailableDay` |

Arguments are parsed with Zod before any service sees them, because a model will
occasionally send `"tomorrow"` where a date was specified. **The worst a confused
model can do** is call the wrong tool with bad arguments and get a validation
error back.

Clinic facts come from retrieval, never memory: a full-text query over
`clinic_knowledge` blended with trigram similarity for typos. No vector store —
the corpus is 21 short documents, and an embedding pipeline would add a network
hop, an API key and a re-indexing step for retrieval quality that is no better
at this size.

---

## Notes

**Availability is computed server-side.** Opening hours live in a `clinic_hours`
table, not in code. The browser holds no schedule of its own — it renders
whatever the availability endpoint returns, so the calendar can never offer a
time the API would refuse.

**Chat is a socket, not a poll.** A turn involves retrieval, tool calls and a
model round trip. Over Socket.IO the typing indicator starts the moment work
begins and the reply lands the moment it finishes. An HTTP fallback runs the
identical chat service.

**Conversations outlive the tab.** Transcripts live in PostgreSQL. A returning
patient resumes their last conversation — on any device — so the assistant still
has the context of what they asked before.

**Authorisation is server-side.** Every `/api/admin/*` request re-reads the user
and checks the role. The route guards in the browser are a courtesy; deleting
them yields a page that renders empty and fills with 403s.

| Browser checks | 50 — both themes, desktop and mobile |

| Contrast | 0 WCAG AA failures across 5 pages × 2 themes |

Run them with `npm run test:e2e` in `backend/`, with the API running.
